name: Aztec
origin: Central Mexico, the Mexica and Nahua world
line: Give thanks, make flower and song, and ask what is truly rooted.

quote.text: Is it true that one lives with roots on the earth? Not forever on earth, only a little while here.
quote.source: Cantares mexicanos, trans. after Miguel León-Portilla

quotes.text: Though it be jade, it falls and shatters; though it be gold, it wears away; though it be quetzal plumage, it is torn asunder. Not forever on earth, only a little while here.
quotes.source: Cantares mexicanos, trans. after Miguel León-Portilla

quotes.text: The wise one: a light, a torch, a stout torch that does not smoke.
quotes.source: Florentine Codex, Book 10, on the tlamatini, trans. after León-Portilla

quotes.text: Broken spears lie in the roads; we have torn our hair in our grief. The houses are roofless now, and their walls are red with blood.
quotes.source: Cantares mexicanos, in The Broken Spears, trans. Lysander Kemp

quotes.text: Father, do not be alarmed; we are still in nepantla.
quotes.by: A Nahua man to Diego Durán, as reported
quotes.source: Diego Durán, History of the Indies of New Spain, 16th century; reported wording

words.usage: Still said in Nahuatl-speaking communities today. A way to thank for a gift or a meal.

words.meaning: The language of the Mexica and many other peoples; "clear sound"
words.usage: Spoken today by well over a million people in Mexico.

words.meaning: The people of Tenochtitlan; the origin of the name Mexico
words.usage: What the people of Tenochtitlan called themselves. "Aztec" is a later, outside term.

words.meaning: The island capital of the Mexica
words.usage: Founded in a lake in the fourteenth century. Mexico City stands on its site.
A pair of words used for poetry and for the expression of truth.
A symbol of beauty, life and also of brevity.
Sung poetry accompanied by drums.
The root of "atlatl" and of many place names.
The ground one stands on and is rooted in.
The sun, and the god who carries it across the sky.
The root of the name Mexico in some interpretations, "navel of the moon", a popular but disputed reading.
A word used also as a modern given name.
Also one of the twenty day signs.

words.meaning: A neighbourhood or kin group; "big house"
words.usage: The basic unit of city life, which held land and organised work, schooling and ritual.

words.meaning: A wise person; one who knows things
words.usage: Plural tlamatinime. Teachers, poets and thinkers.
A king as "one who speaks". Moctezuma was huey tlatoani, great speaker.

words.meaning: Words of the elders; formal speeches of counsel
words.usage: Long, polished addresses given at births, weddings and farewells.
The condition of being well rooted. In León-Portilla’s reading, a key word for truth.

words.meaning: On the earth; the slippery place
words.usage: The poets’ name for the world of the living, where one can slip.
A word for being between two states. Used again in modern thought.
A hard term to translate: not "god" as in Europe. Scholars debate its meaning.
A day sign and the principle of change that animates the world.
The underworld to which most people travelled after death.
The origin of the Mexican word "tianguis", still used for street markets.

words.meaning: A raised field built in a shallow lake
words.usage: Still farmed in Xochimilco. Very productive.
Maize dough steamed in a leaf. The Spanish word tamal comes from it.
The bitter, frothed drink of cacao, maize and spices.
The daily bread of Mesoamerica.
A day sign and a title of warriors.
A day sign and a title of warriors, as in Cuauhtémoc, "descending eagle".

words.meaning: A precious green feather; the quetzal bird’s tail feather
words.usage: Prized for its colour and a symbol of beauty and preciousness.
A year of 365 days: eighteen months of twenty days and five extra days.
Twenty day signs combined with thirteen numbers. Used for naming and divination.

practices.name: Tlazohcamati: thanks before eating
practices.instructions: Before your first meal, pause for a moment. Look at the food. Name where it came from: the plant, the farm, the person who cooked or sold it. If it contains maize, beans, chilli or cacao, remember that these foods came from Mesoamerican farmers. Say "tlazohcamati", thank you, aloud or silently. Then eat slowly. Do not pretend this is an Aztec ritual. It is a small habit of gratitude shaped by a culture that held maize sacred.
practices.why: In Nahua life maize was a central gift, and the daily meal was a point of contact with the land and the people who worked it. Thanks before eating keeps that relation alive.
variations: Do it at every meal for one day.
Write down the origin of one ingredient.
Thank the person who made the meal.

practices.name: Flower and song
practices.instructions: Write a short poem of four to eight lines about something fleeting: a flower, light on a wall, a conversation, a feeling. Use plain images. Read it aloud once, as if it were a song. Do not edit it for approval. If you like, learn two lines of a Nahuatl poem in translation and say them slowly.
practices.why: The Nahua called poetry "flower and song" and treated it as the best way to approach truth, because what is true is beautiful and brief. Making a small poem each day keeps both in view.
variations: Write it on paper and leave it somewhere for a stranger.
Make a drum rhythm to accompany it with a table or a pot.
Choose a flower, look at it for five minutes, then write.

practices.name: Rooted
practices.instructions: Stand barefoot on earth, grass or a floor. Feel the weight of your body on the ground. Breathe slowly for five minutes. Ask yourself the question the Nahua poets asked: what is truly rooted in my life, and what is slippery? Name one of each. Then take one slow step with attention, and go on with your day.
practices.why: Nahua thinkers called the world "the slippery place" and prized neltiliztli, being well rooted. The question helps separate what holds from what only looks solid.
variations: Stand beside a tree and place a hand on the trunk.
Write the two lists in a notebook.

practices.name: Cacao in the evening
practices.instructions: Make a small cup of unsweetened or lightly sweetened hot cacao, with a little cinnamon or chilli if you like. Sit with it. Smell it before you taste. Take small sips for ten to fifteen minutes with no screen. Think about the long journey of the bean, from the forests of Mesoamerica to your hands. If you cannot have caffeine, use a cup of warm water with a little maize flour or just notice the warmth of the cup.
practices.why: Cacao was a drink of honour in Mesoamerica and the beans were used as currency. Taking time with it connects the habit of an evening drink to a very old tradition of hospitality.
variations: Make atole, a warm maize drink, instead.
Read a short passage of poetry while you drink.

practices.name: Words of advice
practices.instructions: Write or speak a short piece of advice to a younger person, a child, or your younger self. Start with "My child…" or "Listen…". Be plain and warm. Include one thing about speaking truthfully and one about working well. Read it aloud once.
practices.why: The huehuetlahtolli were formal speeches of counsel handed down in Nahuatl, given by elders at births, marriages and other turning points of a life.
variations: Write the advice an elder gave you.

tasks.name: Learn five words of Nahuatl
tasks.meta: Thank you, water, house, flower, song

tasks.name: Make or buy a handmade tortilla
Look at a map of Lake Texcoco and Mexico City
Read a chapter of The Broken Spears
Look at the Sun Stone (Piedra del Sol)
Journal: what is truly rooted in your life?
Write about “Rootedness” in your own words

rules.why: Food came from many hands and from the land. A moment of thanks is the smallest form of respect.
The huehuetlatolli, the counsel of elders, repeatedly warn the young to measure their words. A careful speaker is trusted.

rules.text: Tend the place where you live
rules.why: Households, streets and neighbourhoods were organised by calpulli. A tidy place is a sign of a tidy community.

rules.text: Put the group before the self
rules.why: In the calpulli each person owed work and care to the others. Choose one act each day that serves the group.
The Nahua remembered ancestors with food, flowers and songs. Say the name of someone who has died.

rules.text: Do not claim what belongs to living communities
rules.why: Many Nahua communities keep their ceremonies private. Learn and respect without imitating what is not yours.

read.title: The Broken Spears: The Aztec Account of the Conquest of Mexico
read.creator: Miguel León-Portilla, trans. Lysander Kemp
read.why: Nahua accounts of the conquest from the 1500s, translated from Nahuatl.

read.title: Aztec Thought and Culture
read.creator: Miguel León-Portilla
read.why: A classic study of Nahua philosophy and poetry.

read.title: Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs
read.creator: Camilla Townsend
read.why: A history drawn largely from Nahuatl sources written by Nahua authors.

read.title: Aztecs: An Interpretation
read.creator: Inga Clendinnen
read.why: A thoughtful reading of Mexica society and its sacrificial culture.

read.title: The Florentine Codex, trans. Arthur Anderson and Charles Dibble
read.creator: Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua collaborators
read.why: A twelve-book encyclopaedia of Nahua life, recorded with the help of Nahua scholars.

read.title: Flower and Song: Poems of the Aztec Peoples
read.creator: Translated by Edward Kissam and Michael Schmidt

watch.title: Coco
watch.creator: Lee Unkrich and Adrian Molina
watch.why: An animated film set during Mexico’s Day of the Dead. Not about the Aztecs, but about a living culture that holds memory of the dead dear.

listen.title: Xochipilli: An Imagined Aztec Music
listen.creator: Carlos Chávez
listen.why: A composition for winds and percussion that recreates the sound of a pre-Hispanic ensemble.

art.title: The Sun Stone (Piedra del Sol)
art.creator: Mexica sculptors
art.why: A basalt disc nearly four metres across, found in Mexico City in 1790 and kept in the National Museum of Anthropology.

art.title: Coyolxauhqui Stone
art.creator: Mexica sculptors
art.why: A huge carved disc of the dismembered goddess, found at the Templo Mayor in 1978.

art.title: Codex Mendoza
art.creator: Nahua artists
art.why: A painted manuscript of the Aztec empire, its tribute and daily life, made for the Spanish king.

art.title: Templo Mayor Museum
art.creator: Mexico City
art.why: The ruins and finds of the main temple, beside the cathedral in the heart of the city.

art.title: Tenochtitlan murals
art.creator: Diego Rivera
art.why: Murals in the National Palace showing the market and life of the Mexica city.

eat.title: Tamales
eat.creator: Maize dough steamed in leaves, plain or filled
eat.why: A food of everyday and celebration for thousands of years.

eat.title: Tortillas with beans
eat.creator: Fresh maize flatbread
eat.why: The foundation of the Mexican table.

eat.title: Nopales
eat.creator: Prickly pear pads, grilled or in salad
eat.why: A green vegetable of the high plateau.

eat.title: Amaranth sweets
eat.creator: Puffed amaranth with honey
eat.why: Amaranth was a sacred grain. The sweet, called alegría, is still sold in markets.

eat.title: Chapulines
eat.creator: Seasoned grasshoppers
eat.why: A traditional protein-rich snack, eaten especially in Oaxaca.

drink.title: Hot chocolate
drink.creator: Cacao, water or milk, cinnamon and a little chilli
drink.why: Related to the xocolatl of Mesoamerica, which was bitter and frothy.

drink.title: Atole
drink.creator: A warm maize drink
drink.why: Thick, soft and comforting, often flavoured with cinnamon or chocolate.

drink.title: Pulque
drink.creator: Fermented sap of the agave
drink.why: An old drink with strong ceremonial and social roots. Alcoholic, so optional.

customs.title: Say tlazohcamati
customs.creator: Thank in Nahuatl
customs.why: A phrase still used in Nahua communities.

customs.title: Visit a market
customs.creator: Walk through a tianguis
customs.why: Markets have been centres of life since Tenochtitlan’s time.

customs.title: Build a Day of the Dead altar
customs.creator: Marigolds, photographs, food, candles
customs.why: A living Mexican tradition with indigenous and Catholic roots. Marigolds, cempasúchil, are named from a Nahuatl phrase meaning "twenty flower".

customs.title: Name the day
customs.creator: Know which weekday and month it is
customs.why: The Mexica named their days and months. Pay attention to yours.

ethics.title: Moderation
ethics.text: The huehuetlatolli, the formal counsel passed from parents to children, teach moderation in food, speech, pleasure and ambition. The middle way keeps the community whole.
ethics.practice: Choose one thing to do in measure today.

ethics.title: Service to the community
ethics.text: The calpulli gave land and asked for work in return. Leaders were called speakers and judged by how they served.
ethics.practice: Perform one task that serves a group without taking credit.

ethics.title: Humility before the large cycles
ethics.text: The Mexica believed the world had been created and destroyed more than once, and that life depends on a constant exchange of energy. Pride was dangerous.
ethics.practice: Spend a minute looking at the sky and remembering how small a day is.

ethics.title: Respect for elders
ethics.text: Elders carried the words of the past. Young people were taught to listen carefully and to answer with a measured voice.
ethics.practice: Ask an older person to tell you a story and listen without interrupting.

ethics.title: Skill as a moral good
ethics.text: Artists and craftspeople were honoured for making things well. The Toltec ideal was of a person who gives life to their materials.
ethics.practice: Do one task today with unusual care.

ethics.title: Memory of the dead
ethics.text: The Nahua remembered those who died with food, flowers and song, and their descendants still do. Keeping the dead in memory is a duty.
ethics.practice: Light a candle or say a name for someone who died.

philosophy.title: Rootedness
philosophy.text: Nahua thinkers asked how a person could stand firmly on a slippery earth. The word neltiliztli suggests being well rooted and true. A life is rooted when what one says, does and believes line up.
philosophy.practice: Check one belief against what you did today.

philosophy.title: Flower and song
philosophy.text: The poets believed that on earth only poetry could say something true about what is fleeting. Flower and song were not decoration but a way of knowing.
philosophy.practice: Describe something in two images instead of a long explanation.

philosophy.title: The Five Suns
philosophy.text: The Mexica told that the world had passed through four ages, each ended by a catastrophe, and that they lived in the Fifth Sun, called Nahui Ollin, Four Movement, which would end in earthquakes. Time is cyclical and fragile.
philosophy.practice: Notice the age you are living through and what it asks of you.

philosophy.title: Reciprocity
philosophy.text: According to myth the gods sacrificed themselves so that the sun could move. People owed a debt in return, expressed as offerings. The idea of debt to the cosmos shaped Mexica religion and also justified its violence.
philosophy.practice: Name something you have received that you can give back.

philosophy.title: Nepantla
philosophy.text: The word means "in the middle". After the conquest Nahua people lived between two worlds. Today it is used to speak of living between cultures and between states.
philosophy.practice: Name two places or identities you stand between, and one thing each gives.

philosophy.title: The two in one
philosophy.text: León-Portilla argued that Nahua thinkers imagined a dual principle behind all things, Ometeotl. Other scholars question this reading. Either way, the idea of a unity that contains two poles, male and female, light and dark, is a powerful one.
philosophy.practice: Hold two opposites in mind and notice how each depends on the other.

philosophy.title: Teyolia, tonalli, ihiyotl
philosophy.text: Nahua thought described a person as having several centres of life: one in the heart, one in the head, one in the liver. A person is a dynamic combination, not a single soul. Scholars such as Alfredo López Austin explored this.
philosophy.practice: Notice whether a decision today came from the head, the heart or the gut.

philosophy.title: The day as a person
philosophy.text: Each day in the sacred count had a name and a character. Children were named for the day of their birth. Time was personal.
philosophy.practice: Give today a name that describes its character.

philosophy.title: Beauty and brevity
philosophy.text: Jade, gold and feathers are precious but wear away. The poets accepted impermanence and still said that beauty matters.
philosophy.practice: Look at something beautiful that you know will not last.

philosophy.title: The conquest remembered
philosophy.text: Nahua writers recorded their own accounts of the fall of Tenochtitlan, in their language and writing. Their histories insist that the conquered had voices and a version of what happened.
philosophy.practice: Read one account of an event from the point of view of those who lost.

Where did you find roots in your own life?

guide.origin: The Valley of Mexico and the wider Nahua world of central Mexico
intro: The people we call the Aztecs called themselves Mexica. Their capital Tenochtitlan stood on an island in the middle of Lake Texcoco, where Mexico City stands today. Founded, according to tradition, in 1325, it grew into one of the largest cities in the world by 1519, with a population estimated at between 200,000 and 300,000. Its markets, causeways, canals and raised gardens astonished the Spanish who first saw it.

The Mexica spoke Nahuatl, a language still spoken by well over a million people. Their empire, in reality a Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed in 1428, controlled much of central Mexico through tribute rather than direct rule. Their religion centred on a universe in motion, a Fifth Sun that needed to be fed, and gods linked to maize, rain, war and the sun. Sacrifice, including human sacrifice, was a part of it, and it must be neither ignored nor made the whole story.

They were also poets, painters, astronomers, farmers and philosophers. Teachers at the calpulli schools taught boys and girls to speak well, to work and to behave. The Nahua sages, tlamatinime, thought about truth, rootedness, change and the brevity of life. The poet-king Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco is remembered for songs about the fragility of jade and gold.

In 1519 Hernán Cortés arrived with a few hundred Spaniards and, crucially, with thousands of indigenous allies who resented Mexica rule. Smallpox, introduced the next year, killed a large share of the population. After a siege of several months Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521. Within decades, the city was rebuilt as the capital of New Spain.

What we know of Mexica life comes from several sources: their own painted books, archaeology, and accounts written in Spanish or Nahuatl after the conquest by friars and by Nahua scholars. These sources are valuable and also shaped by their authors, especially by Spanish interests. This Onda draws on them with care.

Nahua people did not disappear. Millions of their descendants live in Mexico and beyond, speaking Nahuatl, farming maize, keeping festivals and writing poetry. This Onda offers gratitude, poetry, rootedness and a slow cup of cacao, in a spirit of respect. It does not recreate ceremony and invites you to learn from Nahua people themselves.

figures.name: Nezahualcoyotl
figures.bio: Ruler of Texcoco, builder of aqueducts and dikes, and a poet. Many songs are attributed to him, though some were probably composed later.

figures.name: Tlacaelel
figures.bio: Adviser to several Mexica rulers and a reorganiser of state religion and history. His real influence is debated.

figures.name: Moctezuma II
figures.bio: Huey tlatoani from 1502, who met Cortés in 1519 and died in 1520 in circumstances that are disputed.

figures.name: Cuauhtémoc
figures.bio: The last Mexica ruler, who led the defence of Tenochtitlan and was captured in 1521. Executed by Cortés in 1525.

figures.name: Malintzin
figures.bio: A Nahua woman given to the Spaniards in 1519 who served as interpreter and adviser to Cortés. Her role is still debated in Mexico.

figures.name: Bernardino de Sahagún
figures.bio: Franciscan friar who, with Nahua scholars, compiled the Florentine Codex, an encyclopaedia of Nahua life.

figures.name: Diego Durán
figures.bio: A Dominican friar who wrote a long history of the Aztecs based on Nahua informants.

figures.name: Antonio Valeriano
figures.bio: A Nahua scholar and Latinist at the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, who helped Sahagún and later became governor of Tenochtitlan.

figures.name: Miguel León-Portilla
figures.bio: Mexican historian who translated and championed Nahua literature and philosophy. Author of The Broken Spears and Aztec Thought and Culture.

figures.name: Inga Clendinnen
figures.bio: Australian historian whose Aztecs: An Interpretation, 1991, reads Mexica ritual and daily life with close attention to the sources.

history.detail: According to tradition the Mexica, long wanderers, founded their city on an island in Lake Texcoco after seeing an eagle on a cactus, a sign promised by their god. Archaeology confirms a city from this period.
Acamapichtli became the first ruler of Tenochtitlan, allied through marriage with the Culhua dynasty, whose prestige the Mexica needed.
Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan defeated Azcapotzalco and formed an alliance that grew into the largest state in the Valley of Mexico and beyond.
The reign of Moctezuma Ilhuicamina saw expansion, a stronger bureaucracy and the growth of the Templo Mayor.
The expanded main temple of Tenochtitlan was dedicated during the reign of Ahuitzotl. Claims about the number sacrificed vary widely and are doubted by some historians.
The ninth tlatoani extended the empire and surrounded himself with ceremony. He faced rebellion among subject peoples and then the arrival of the Spaniards.
Hernán Cortés landed on the coast, formed alliances with peoples such as the Tlaxcalans, and entered Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519.
The Spaniards were driven from the city on the night of 30 June. In the same year a smallpox epidemic killed a large share of the people of the valley.
After a siege of about three months by the Spanish and tens of thousands of indigenous allies, Cuauhtémoc surrendered and the city was destroyed.
The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco opened to train sons of Nahua nobles, who became scholars, translators and informants.
Sahagún and his Nahua collaborators gathered material on Nahua life in twelve books, written in Nahuatl with Spanish translation and paintings.
Workers repairing the Zócalo in Mexico City unearthed the great carved disc known as the Sun Stone.
Electrical workers discovered the carved disc of the dismembered goddess, prompting excavation of the Templo Mayor.

concepts.text: Poetry as the way to truth.
concepts.detail: In xochitl in cuicatl was the Nahua name for poetry. Flowers and songs were beautiful, brief and sensory, which made them fit tools for speaking about a world that is itself fleeting. In the poems, they carry grief, joy and philosophical questions.

León-Portilla read the word as linked to the idea of being well rooted, and so of truth. The poets asked whether anyone is truly rooted on earth. The question frames a search for what can stand firm in a changing world.

concepts.text: The Mexica story of successive ages.
concepts.detail: The Mexica believed that the world had passed through four previous suns, each destroyed, and that they lived in the fifth, Nahui Ollin, which had been set in motion by the sacrifice of the gods. It must be sustained by offerings, so that the cycle continues.
Each calpulli held land, ran a local school, kept its own temple and sent men to work and fight. It was the place where a person had belonging, duties and protection.

Formal speeches given at births, weddings and other moments, collected by Sahagún. They teach moderation, respect, speech and responsibility in a rich, formal language that Nahuatl speakers still admire.
Sages who studied the painted books, the calendar, the stars and poetry. The Florentine Codex describes the ideal wise person as a light and a torch that does not smoke, a guide for others.

concepts.text: A solar year and a sacred count.
concepts.detail: The xiuhpohualli counted 365 days in 18 months of 20 days plus five extra days. The tonalpohualli counted 260 days, combining 20 day signs with 13 numbers. Every 52 years the two came back into step, and the Mexica marked the date with a New Fire ceremony.

The Mexica believed that the gods created the sun through self-sacrifice, so humans owe offerings in return. The idea shaped ritual life and justified the sacrifice of captives, a practice that Spanish accounts exaggerated and archaeology confirms.

The word appears in a sixteenth-century report in which a Nahua man says people are still in the middle, between old and new faiths. It has since been used by scholars, especially Chicana thinkers such as Gloria Anzaldúa, to describe living between worlds.
Farmers built rectangular plots in shallow lakes from layers of mud and vegetation, held by willow trees. They gave several harvests a year and fed a large city. A few are still farmed in Xochimilco.

facts.text: English words that came from Nahuatl through Spanish include tomato, avocado, chilli, coyote, tamale, chocolate and guacamole.
The Sun Stone weighs about 24 tonnes and is nearly 3.6 metres across. It is not a calendar in the way often claimed, and scholars still discuss its purpose.
Cacao beans were used as a currency across Mesoamerica, and counterfeiters made fake beans out of clay and dough.
The chinampa gardens of Xochimilco and the historic centre of Mexico City have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
Nahuatl is spoken today by more than 1.6 million people, according to Mexico’s 2020 census.
Tenochtitlan was connected to the shore by three long causeways and supplied by aqueducts from Chapultepec. Nezahualcoyotl is credited with building a long dike across the lake to control floods.
The marigold flower used at Day of the Dead, cempasúchil, takes its name from Nahuatl words for twenty and flower.

sensitivity.note: The Mexica and other Nahua peoples built a great civilisation, and their descendants live today. This Onda offers gratitude, poetry and reflection inspired by Nahua thought. It does not reproduce ceremonies, and it treats the sacrificial side of Mexica religion as part of an honest history.
requiredCaveats: "Aztec" is an outside term. The people of Tenochtitlan called themselves Mexica, and many Nahua peoples shared the language. Use the name that people use for themselves when you can.
Much of what we know comes from Spanish friars and colonial sources. Read accounts of sacrifice and of conquest with that in mind, and prefer Nahua-authored texts where you can.
Ceremonies such as danza, copal blessings, temazcal steam baths and Day of the Dead rites belong to living communities. Attend only when invited and do not imitate them as costume.
This content has not yet been reviewed by Nahua speakers, Mexican historians or community members. It should be before release.
